Physiology-03.question: ১) Effect of Antidiuretic hormone
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is H₂O reabsorption. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also called vasopressin, increases water reabsorption in the kidney by increasing aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting ducts.

Mechanism:

  • ADH binds to V2 receptors on collecting duct cells

  • Activates cAMP pathway

  • Inserts aquaporin-2 water channels

  • ↑ Water reabsorption → ↓ urine volume

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Na⁺ reabsorption ✗ → Mainly regulated by aldosterone.

  • K⁺ reabsorption ✗ → Mainly influenced by aldosterone and renal handling mechanisms.

  • Cl⁻ reabsorption ✗ → Not the primary action of ADH.

High-yield Endocrine recall:

Hormone Main renal action
ADH ↑ Water reabsorption
Aldosterone ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption, ↑ K⁺ excretion
PTH ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption

Exam pearl:
ADH = water conservation hormone → aquaporin insertion → concentrated urine.

Physiology-03.question: ২) Hormones secreted by kidneys excludes
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Epinephrine. Epinephrine (adrenaline) is secreted by the adrenal medulla, not the kidney.

Kidney produces/secretes:

  • Erythropoietin ✓

    • Stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow

  • Prostaglandins ✓

    • Regulate renal blood flow and salt/water handling

  • Thrombopoietin ✓ (mainly produced by liver, but also associated with renal production in small amounts)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Erythropoietin → Produced by renal interstitial cells in response to hypoxia.

  • Thrombopoietin → Mainly produced by the liver; kidney can contribute.

  • Prostaglandins → Synthesized in the kidney.

High-yield Renal endocrine recall:

Hormone/substance Main source
Erythropoietin Kidney
Renin Kidney
Calcitriol (active vitamin D) Kidney
Prostaglandins Kidney
Epinephrine Adrenal medulla

Exam pearl:
Kidney = EPO + Renin + Calcitriol; Epinephrine = Adrenal medulla.

Physiology-03.question: ৩) Interstitial fluid is an ultrafiltrate of
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is plasma. Interstitial fluid is an ultrafiltrate of plasma that forms when fluid passes through capillary walls into the extracellular space.

Key points:

  • Plasma is filtered across capillary walls.

  • The filtrate becomes interstitial fluid.

  • It contains water, electrolytes, nutrients, and small molecules but has very little protein compared with plasma.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Total body fluid ✗ → Includes both intracellular and extracellular fluids; not the source of interstitial fluid.

  • ICF (intracellular fluid) ✗ → Present inside cells and not involved in formation of interstitial fluid.

  • Protein ✗ → Proteins are mainly retained in plasma and are not the source of interstitial fluid.

High-yield Fluid compartment recall:

Fluid Origin
Interstitial fluid Ultrafiltrate of plasma
Plasma Intravascular fluid
ICF Fluid inside cells

Exam pearl:
Plasma → capillary filtration → interstitial fluid → lymphatic return.

Physiology-03.question: ৪) Substances completely reabsorbed by kidney
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Glucose. Under normal physiological conditions, filtered glucose is completely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, so it is absent in urine.

Renal handling:

  • Glucose ✓

    • 100% reabsorbed (up to renal threshold) by proximal tubule

  • Bicarbonate ✗

    • Mostly reabsorbed (~80–90%) but not considered completely.

  • Urea ✗

    • Partially reabsorbed and contributes to medullary osmotic gradient.

  • Sodium ✗

    • Reabsorbed extensively (~99%) but not completely.

High-yield Renal recall:

Substance Renal handling
Glucose Completely reabsorbed (normal)
Sodium Almost completely reabsorbed
Bicarbonate Mostly reabsorbed
Urea Partially reabsorbed

Exam pearl:
Normal urine contains no glucose because filtered glucose is completely reabsorbed.

Physiology-03.question: ৫) Which is not a part of JG apparatus?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Podocyte. Podocytes are part of the glomerular filtration barrier, not the juxtaglomerular (JG) apparatus.

Components of Juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA):

  • Macula densa ✓

    • Specialized cells of distal tubule sensing NaCl concentration

  • Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells ✓

    • Modified smooth muscle cells of afferent arteriole secreting renin

  • Extraglomerular mesangial cells (lacis cells) ✓

    • Support and transmit signals within JGA

Podocytes ✗

  • Located in the visceral layer of Bowman’s capsule

  • Form filtration slits for glomerular filtration

High-yield Renal recall:

Structure Function
Macula densa Detects tubular NaCl
JG cells Renin secretion
Extraglomerular mesangial cells Signal transmission
Podocytes Glomerular filtration barrier

Exam pearl:
JGA = Macula densa + JG cells + extraglomerular mesangial cells.

Physiology-03.question: ৬) The average blood volume of adults is about ... litres?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 5 litres. The average blood volume of an adult human is approximately 5 litres.

Key points:

  • Blood volume ≈ 7% of body weight

  • Average adult:

    • Male: ~5–6 L

    • Female: ~4–5 L

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 7 litres ✗ → Higher than normal average adult blood volume.

  • 9 litres ✗ → Excessively high.

  • 10 litres ✗ → Not a physiological value.

High-yield Physiology recall:

Parameter Approximate value
Adult blood volume ~5 L
Plasma volume ~3 L
RBC volume ~2 L

Exam pearl:
Average adult blood volume = about 5 litres (≈70 mL/kg).

Physiology-03.question: ৭) Substances that freely filtered but not reabsorbed by the kidney -
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Inulin. Inulin is freely filtered by the glomerulus and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the kidney, making it the gold standard marker for measuring glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

Renal handling:

  • Inulin ✓

    • Freely filtered

    • Not reabsorbed

    • Not secreted

    • Used to measure GFR

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Urea ✗ → Freely filtered but partially reabsorbed in the renal tubules.

  • Glucose ✗ → Freely filtered and completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule (normally).

  • Bicarbonate ✗ → Freely filtered and mostly reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.

High-yield Renal recall:

Substance Filtered Reabsorbed Use
Inulin Yes No GFR measurement
Glucose Yes Complete Energy substrate
Urea Yes Partial Nitrogen waste
Bicarbonate Yes Mostly Acid-base balance

Exam pearl:
Inulin clearance = true GFR because it is filtered only.

Physiology-03.question: ৮) Most of the absorption takes place in
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is PCT. The proximal convoluted tubule is the major site of renal reabsorption, where most filtered substances are reabsorbed back into the blood.

Functions of PCT:

  • Reabsorbs ~65–70% of filtered Na⁺ and water

  • 100% glucose (normally)

  • 100% amino acids (normally)

  • Most bicarbonate

  • Significant amounts of chloride, potassium, and phosphate

The other options are incorrect because:

  • DCT (Distal Convoluted Tubule) ✗ → Fine regulation of sodium, calcium, and acid-base balance.

  • Loop of Henle (LOH) ✗ → Establishes medullary concentration gradient; important for water and salt handling.

  • Collecting duct (CD) ✗ → Final regulation of water balance under ADH control.

High-yield Renal recall:

Nephron segment Main function
PCT Bulk reabsorption (~65–70%)
Loop of Henle Concentration of urine
DCT Fine adjustment
Collecting duct ADH-mediated water reabsorption

Exam pearl:
PCT = powerhouse of renal reabsorption.

Physiology-03.question: ৯) The glomerular capillaries cannot filtrate...?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is plasma protein. The glomerular filtration barrier normally prevents large plasma proteins (especially albumin) from passing into the filtrate.

Glomerular filtration barrier:

  • Fenestrated endothelium

  • Basement membrane

  • Podocyte filtration slits

Substances that are freely filtered:

  • Glucose ✓

  • Sodium ✓

  • Creatinine ✓ (freely filtered; slight tubular secretion)

Plasma proteins ✗

  • Large size and negative charge prevent filtration under normal conditions.

High-yield Renal recall:

Substance Filtration
Glucose Freely filtered
Na⁺ Freely filtered
Creatinine Freely filtered
Plasma protein (albumin) Not filtered normally

Exam pearl:
Normal urine has no significant protein because the glomerulus retains plasma proteins.

Physiology-03.question: ১০) Net filtration pressure ___mm Hg
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 18 mm Hg. Net filtration pressure (NFP) in the glomerulus is approximately 10 mm Hg in many modern texts, but in classic renal physiology MCQs it is often calculated as 18 mm Hg.

Calculation (classic values):

NFP = Glomerular hydrostatic pressure − (Blood colloid osmotic pressure + Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure)

= 60 − (32 + 10)
= 18 mm Hg

Where:

  • Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure = 60 mm Hg

  • Plasma colloid osmotic pressure = 32 mm Hg

  • Bowman’s capsule pressure = 10 mm Hg

High-yield Renal recall:

Pressure Value
Glomerular hydrostatic pressure 60 mm Hg
Plasma oncotic pressure 32 mm Hg
Bowman’s capsule pressure 10 mm Hg
Net filtration pressure 18 mm Hg

Exam pearl:
NFP = 60 − (32 + 10) = 18 mm Hg (classic physiology value).

Physiology-03.question: ১১) The percentage of TBW in new-borns
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 70%. In newborns, total body water (TBW) constitutes approximately 70% of body weight.

Total body water changes with age:

Age group TBW (% body weight)
Newborn ~70%
Adult male ~60%
Adult female ~50–55%
Elderly ~45–50%

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 40% ✗ → Seen in elderly/dehydrated states.

  • 50% ✗ → Approximate adult female value.

  • 60% ✗ → Approximate adult male value.

High-yield Fluid physiology recall:

Newborn → 70% water
Adult male → 60% water
Adult female → 50–55% water

Exam pearl:
Higher body water content in newborns = ~70% of body weight.

Physiology-03.question: ১২) Renin is secreted from
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Juxtaglomerular cells. Renin is secreted by modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole called juxtaglomerular (JG) cells.

Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS):

  • ↓ Renal perfusion pressure → JG cells release renin

  • Renin converts angiotensinogen → angiotensin I

  • ACE converts angiotensin I → angiotensin II

  • Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone secretion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Macula densa ✗ → Detects NaCl concentration in distal tubule and signals JG cells to release renin.

  • Mesangial cells ✗ → Provide structural support and help transmit signals.

  • Lacis cells (extraglomerular mesangial cells) ✗ → Part of JGA but do not secrete renin.

High-yield Renal recall:

JGA component Function
Juxtaglomerular cells Renin secretion
Macula densa NaCl sensing
Lacis cells Signal transmission

Exam pearl:
Renin = JG cells of afferent arteriole.

Physiology-03.question: ১৩) Renal autoregulation is important to maintain the
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is GFR (Glomerular Filtration Rate). Renal autoregulation maintains a relatively constant GFR despite changes in systemic blood pressure.

Mechanisms of renal autoregulation:

  • Myogenic mechanism

    • Afferent arteriole constricts or dilates in response to pressure changes.

  • Tubuloglomerular feedback

    • Macula densa regulates afferent arteriole tone based on tubular NaCl delivery.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • RPF (Renal plasma flow) ✗ → May change with blood pressure; autoregulation primarily maintains GFR.

  • BP (Blood pressure) ✗ → Regulated mainly by cardiovascular and neuroendocrine systems.

  • Osmolarity ✗ → Controlled by ADH and renal concentrating mechanisms.

High-yield Renal recall:

Process Main function
Renal autoregulation Maintain GFR
ADH Maintain water balance/osmolality
RAAS Maintain BP and volume

Exam pearl:
Renal autoregulation keeps GFR constant over a wide range of blood pressures.

Physiology-03.question: ১৪) Beriberi occur in deficiency of
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Thiamine (Vitamin B₁). Beriberi occurs due to deficiency of thiamine, which is essential for carbohydrate metabolism and normal nerve and cardiac function.

Types of beriberi:

  • Dry beriberi → Peripheral neuropathy, muscle weakness

  • Wet beriberi → High-output cardiac failure, cardiomegaly, edema

  • Infantile beriberi → Occurs in breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Niacin (Vitamin B₃) ✗ → Deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia).

  • Riboflavin (Vitamin B₂) ✗ → Deficiency causes cheilosis, angular stomatitis, glossitis.

  • Biotin (Vitamin B₇) ✗ → Deficiency causes dermatitis and alopecia.

High-yield Vitamin recall:

Vitamin Deficiency disease
B₁ (Thiamine) Beriberi
B₃ (Niacin) Pellagra
B₂ (Riboflavin) Cheilosis, glossitis
B₇ (Biotin) Dermatitis, alopecia

Exam pearl:
Beriberi = Vitamin B₁ (Thiamine) deficiency.

Physiology-03.question: ১৫) Presence of positive benedict's test indicate that there might be a problem in
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is PCT. A positive Benedict’s test indicates the presence of reducing sugars (mainly glucose) in urine, suggesting a problem with glucose reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule.

Renal handling of glucose:

  • Glucose is freely filtered at the glomerulus.

  • Normally 100% glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT through sodium-glucose cotransporters.

  • Damage to PCT → impaired glucose reabsorption → glucosuria → positive Benedict’s test.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • DCT ✗ → Mainly involved in electrolyte regulation and acid-base balance.

  • Loop of Henle (LOH) ✗ → Responsible for counter-current mechanism.

  • Collecting duct (CD) ✗ → Regulates final water balance under ADH.

High-yield Renal recall:

Nephron segment Main function
PCT Glucose, amino acid, bicarbonate reabsorption
Loop of Henle Concentration of urine
DCT Fine electrolyte adjustment
Collecting duct ADH-mediated water reabsorption

Exam pearl:
Glucosuria with positive Benedict’s test → think PCT dysfunction or diabetes mellitus.

Physiology-03.question: ১৬) Ghrelin is released by the
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Stomach. Ghrelin is mainly secreted by the stomach, especially the X/A-like cells of the gastric fundus.

Functions of ghrelin:

  • Stimulates hunger and appetite

  • Increases growth hormone (GH) secretion from the anterior pituitary

  • Acts on the hypothalamus to regulate energy balance

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Anterior pituitary gland ✗ → Responds to ghrelin by releasing GH; it does not produce ghrelin.

  • Hypothalamus ✗ → Ghrelin acts here to stimulate appetite but is not the main site of secretion.

  • D cells ✗ → Secrete somatostatin (pancreatic and gastric D cells).

High-yield Endocrine recall:

Hormone Main source
Ghrelin Stomach (fundus)
Leptin Adipose tissue
Somatostatin D cells
Insulin β-cells of pancreas

Exam pearl:
Ghrelin = gastric hunger hormone → secreted mainly by stomach.

Physiology-03.question: ১৭) Limiting pH of urine
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 4.5. The minimum (limiting) pH to which urine can be acidified is approximately 4.5.

Key points:

  • Normal urine pH range: 4.5–8.0

  • Minimum urine pH: ~4.5

  • Maximum urine pH: ~8.0

  • Acidification occurs mainly through:

    • H⁺ secretion by renal tubules

    • Ammonium (NH₄⁺) excretion

    • Titratable acids (phosphate)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 3.5 ✗ → Lower than the physiological limit.

  • 4 ✗ → Below the normal minimum.

  • 5 ✗ → Not the limiting pH.

High-yield Renal recall:

Parameter Value
Normal urine pH 4.5–8
Limiting (minimum) urine pH 4.5

Exam pearl:
Kidney can acidify urine up to a minimum pH of about 4.5.

Physiology-03.question: ১৮) When hunger contractions occur in the stomach, the person sometimes experiences mild pain in the pit of the stomach, called
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Hunger pangs. Hunger pangs are mild epigastric pain sensations caused by strong gastric contractions when the stomach is empty.

Key points:

  • Occur during fasting, usually 12–24 hours after the last meal

  • Caused by increased peristaltic contractions of the empty stomach

  • Associated with the migrating motor complex (MMC)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Acute gastritis ✗ → Inflammation of gastric mucosa causing epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting.

  • Ileus ✗ → Failure of intestinal motility, causing abdominal distension and obstruction-like symptoms.

  • Hunger contractions ✗ → The contractions themselves produce the sensation, but the pain sensation is termed hunger pangs.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Term Meaning
Hunger contractions Strong gastric contractions during fasting
Hunger pangs Pain sensation due to hunger contractions
MMC Cleansing motor activity during fasting

Exam pearl:
Empty stomach contractions causing mild epigastric pain = hunger pan

Physiology-03.question: ১৯) Normally tubular reabsorption is ___ L/day?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 178.5 L/day. The kidneys filter approximately 180 L/day of plasma, and about 99% of this filtrate is reabsorbed back into the blood.

Calculation:

  • Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ≈ 125 mL/min

  • Daily filtration = 125 × 1440 min = ~180 L/day

  • Urine output ≈ 1.5 L/day

  • Tubular reabsorption = 180 − 1.5 = 178.5 L/day

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 1.5 L/day ✗ → Approximate daily urine volume (excretion), not reabsorption.

  • 180 L/day ✗ → Approximate amount filtered, not reabsorbed.

  • 125 L/day ✗ → GFR expressed as mL/min (not daily tubular reabsorption).

High-yield Renal recall:

Parameter Value
GFR ~125 mL/min
Filtrate formed ~180 L/day
Tubular reabsorption ~178.5 L/day
Urine output ~1.5 L/day

Exam pearl:
180 L filtered → 178.5 L reabsorbed → 1.5 L urine/day.

Physiology-03.question: ২০) Activator of pepsinogens
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is HCl (Hydrochloric acid). HCl secreted by gastric parietal cells activates inactive pepsinogen into active pepsin in the stomach.

Mechanism:

  • Chief cells → secrete pepsinogen (inactive enzyme)

  • Parietal cells → secrete HCl

  • HCl converts pepsinogen → pepsin

  • Pepsin then digests proteins

The other options are incorrect because:

  • H⁺ ✗ → H⁺ contributes to the acidic environment, but the physiological activator is HCl.

  • K⁺ ✗ → Not involved in pepsinogen activation.

  • Na⁺ ✗ → Not involved in gastric enzyme activation.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Component Source Function
HCl Parietal cells Activates pepsinogen
Pepsinogen Chief cells Protein digestion precursor
Pepsin Activated enzyme Protein digestion

Exam pearl:
HCl activates pepsinogen → pepsin.

Physiology-03.question: ২১) Micelle formation is necessary for the intestinal absorption of
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Vitamin D. Micelle formation is essential for the intestinal absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and lipids.

Mechanism:

  • Dietary fats are digested into fatty acids and monoglycerides.

  • Bile salts form micelles with these lipid products.

  • Micelles transport lipids and fat-soluble vitamins through the aqueous intestinal environment to the enterocyte surface.

  • Vitamin D is then absorbed into intestinal cells.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Galactose ✗ → Absorbed by SGLT-1 sodium-dependent transporter in enterocytes.

  • Leucine ✗ → Absorbed by amino acid transporters; does not require micelles.

  • Bile acids ✗ → They participate in micelle formation and are absorbed mainly in the terminal ileum, but micelles are primarily required for absorption of lipid-soluble substances.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Substance Absorption mechanism
Vitamin D Micelle-dependent absorption
Glucose/Galactose SGLT-1
Amino acids Specific transporters
Bile acids Enterohepatic circulation

Exam pearl:
Micelles are essential for absorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

Physiology-03.question: ২২) Activator of salivary α-amylase
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Cl⁻ (chloride ion). Chloride is an essential activator of salivary α-amylase (ptyalin), which begins carbohydrate digestion in the mouth.

Key points:

  • Salivary α-amylase is secreted by salivary glands.

  • It requires chloride ions (Cl⁻) for optimal enzymatic activity.

  • It digests starch → maltose and dextrins.

  • It works best at a neutral pH (~6.8).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • H⁺ ✗ → Acidic environment inhibits salivary amylase.

  • K⁺ ✗ → Not the specific activator of salivary α-amylase.

  • Na⁺ ✗ → Present in saliva but does not activate α-amylase.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Enzyme Activator
Salivary α-amylase Cl⁻
Pepsinogen HCl
Pancreatic lipase Colipase + bile salts

Exam pearl:
Chloride activates salivary α-amylase.

Physiology-03.question: ২৩) Kidney synthesize glucose by the process of
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Gluconeogenesis. The kidney can synthesize glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors by gluconeogenesis, especially during prolonged fasting.

Renal gluconeogenesis:

  • Occurs mainly in the renal cortex

  • Uses substrates such as:

    • Lactate

    • Glycerol

    • Glutamine (important in fasting and acid-base regulation)

  • Helps maintain blood glucose levels during starvation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Glycolysis ✗ → Breakdown of glucose to produce energy.

  • Glycogenesis ✗ → Formation of glycogen from glucose (mainly liver and muscle).

  • Glucogenesis ✗ → Not a standard physiological term for glucose synthesis.

High-yield Metabolism recall:

Process Function
Gluconeogenesis New glucose synthesis
Glycolysis Glucose breakdown
Glycogenesis Glycogen formation
Glycogenolysis Glycogen breakdown

Exam pearl:
Kidney cortex + liver = sites of gluconeogenesis.

Physiology-03.question: ২৪) About what % of ICF in human body is fluid?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 40%. Intracellular fluid (ICF) constitutes approximately 40% of total body weight in an average adult.

Body fluid distribution:

  • Total body water (TBW) ≈ 60% of body weight

  • ICF ≈ 40% of body weight (about two-thirds of TBW)

  • ECF ≈ 20% of body weight (about one-third of TBW)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 20% ✗ → Represents extracellular fluid (ECF).

  • 60% ✗ → Represents total body water (TBW).

  • 50% ✗ → Not the standard value for ICF.

High-yield Fluid physiology recall:

Compartment % of body weight
Total body water (TBW) 60%
Intracellular fluid (ICF) 40%
Extracellular fluid (ECF) 20%

Exam pearl:
ICF = 40%, ECF = 20%, TBW = 60% of body weight.

Physiology-03.question: ২৫) Stimuli that inhibit gastrin secretion
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Somatostatin. Somatostatin, secreted by gastric D cells, inhibits gastrin secretion from G cells and reduces gastric acid secretion.

Regulation of gastrin secretion:

Stimulators:

  • Gastric distension ✓

  • Increased vagal discharge (via GRP) ✓

  • Peptides and amino acids ✓

  • Calcium ✓

Inhibitor:

  • Somatostatin ✓

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Distention ✗ → Stimulates gastrin release by activating G cells.

  • Increased vagal discharge ✗ → Stimulates gastrin secretion through gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP).

  • Calcium ✗ → Stimulates gastrin secretion.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Factor Effect on gastrin
Somatostatin ↓ Gastrin
Distension ↑ Gastrin
Vagus (GRP) ↑ Gastrin
Calcium ↑ Gastrin

Exam pearl:
D cells release somatostatin → inhibits G cells → ↓ gastrin → ↓ HCl.

Physiology-03.question: ২৬) Glomerular colloid osmotic pressure (mmHg)
২৭) Fluid output through sweat (ml) in normal condition?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 350 ml. Normal daily fluid loss through sweat is approximately 350 mL/day (insensible loss varies with environmental conditions and activity).

Normal daily water loss:

  • Urine → ~1500 mL/day

  • Skin (sweat + insensible loss) → ~350 mL/day

  • Lungs → ~350 mL/day

  • Feces → ~100 mL/day

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 100 ml ✗ → Approximate fecal water loss.

  • 200 ml ✗ → Lower than normal skin loss.

  • 500 ml ✗ → May occur with increased temperature/exercise but not normal condition.

High-yield Fluid balance recall:

Route Approximate daily loss
Urine 1500 ml
Sweat/skin 350 ml
Lungs 350 ml
Feces 100 ml

Exam pearl:
Normal sweat water loss ≈ 350 mL/day.

Physiology-03.question: ২৮) ICF & ISF are separated by
২৯) Organic substances excreted in urine excludes
৩০) Clearance rate is minimum for
৩১) Which part of renal tubule is never permeable to NaCl?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Thin descending limb. The thin descending limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to water but is essentially impermeable to NaCl.

Characteristics of nephron segments:

Segment Water permeability NaCl permeability
PCT High High
Thin descending limb High Very low/absent
Thin ascending limb Low Permeable to NaCl
Thick ascending limb None Actively transports NaCl

The other options are incorrect because:

  • PCT ✗ → Reabsorbs large amounts of NaCl.

  • Thin ascending limb ✗ → Passive NaCl movement occurs.

  • Thick ascending limb ✗ → Actively reabsorbs NaCl via Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) and is water impermeable.

High-yield Renal recall:

Loop of Henle:

  • Descending limb → Water out

  • Ascending limb → Salt out, no water

Exam pearl:
Thin descending limb = water permeable, NaCl impermeable.

Physiology-03.question: ৩২) Which decreases PO4- reabsorption?
৩৩) Which increases GFR?
৩৪) What is the rate of urine excretion (ml/min)?
৩৫) Which of transporter is used by all of the monosaccharides?
৩৬) Lactase enzyme is derived from
৩৭) Large intestine secretion is devoid of
৩৮) Water content is least in
৩৯) Which one may be acidic?
৪০) Accessory digestive organs exclude
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Pharynx. The pharynx is a part of the alimentary canal, not an accessory digestive organ.

Accessory digestive organs include:

  • Teeth → Mechanical breakdown of food

  • Tongue → Manipulation of food and helps swallowing

  • Salivary glands → Produce saliva containing digestive enzymes

Pharynx ✗

  • A muscular passage shared by the respiratory and digestive systems

  • Helps in swallowing but is part of the GI tract, not an accessory organ

High-yield GI anatomy recall:

Category Examples
Accessory digestive organs Teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas
Alimentary canal Mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, intestine

Exam pearl:
Accessory organs assist digestion but food does not pass through them.

Physiology-03.question: ৪১) Substance that increases salivary secretion
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Acetylcholine. Parasympathetic stimulation through acetylcholine is the main stimulus for salivary secretion, producing a large volume of watery saliva.

Mechanism:

  • Parasympathetic nerves (CN VII and CN IX) release acetylcholine

  • ACh acts on muscarinic receptors of salivary glands

  • Causes increased salivary secretion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ergotamine ✗ → Serotonergic/adrenergic effects; does not increase salivary secretion.

  • Atropine ✗ → Antimuscarinic drug that decreases salivary secretion and causes dry mouth.

  • Chloroform ✗ → Not a physiological stimulator of saliva.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Stimulus Effect on saliva
Acetylcholine (parasympathetic) ↑ Salivary secretion
Sympathetic stimulation Small amount, thick saliva
Atropine ↓ Salivation

Exam pearl:
Parasympathetic ACh = copious watery saliva.

Physiology-03.question: ৪২) Absence of intrinsic factor of castle may lead to
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Pernicious anaemia. Intrinsic factor of Castle, secreted by gastric parietal cells, is required for vitamin B₁₂ absorption in the terminal ileum. Its absence causes vitamin B₁₂ deficiency and pernicious anaemia.

Mechanism:

  • Gastric parietal cells → Intrinsic factor

  • Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B₁₂

  • B₁₂–intrinsic factor complex absorbed in terminal ileum

  • Deficiency → impaired DNA synthesis → megaloblastic anaemia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Iron deficiency anaemia ✗ → Due to iron deficiency, not intrinsic factor deficiency.

  • Haemolytic anaemia ✗ → Due to increased RBC destruction.

  • Sideroblastic anaemia ✗ → Due to defective haem synthesis.

High-yield Haematology recall:

Defect Disease
Intrinsic factor deficiency Pernicious anaemia (B₁₂ deficiency)
Folate deficiency Megaloblastic anaemia
Iron deficiency Microcytic anaemia

Exam pearl:
No intrinsic factor → No B₁₂ absorption → Pernicious anaemia.

Physiology-03.question: ৪৩) Factor stimulating the Secretion of Hydrochloric Acid
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Histamine. Histamine is the most important stimulant of hydrochloric acid (HCl) secretion from gastric parietal cells.

Mechanism:

  • Histamine is released from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the stomach.

  • It binds to H₂ receptors on parietal cells.

  • This stimulates H⁺/K⁺ ATPase → increased gastric acid secretion.

Other stimulators of HCl secretion:

  • Gastrin

  • Acetylcholine (vagal stimulation)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Secretin ✗ → Inhibits gastric acid secretion and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion.

  • Gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP) ✗ → Inhibits gastric acid secretion and motility.

  • Peptide YY ✗ → Reduces gastric motility and secretion after meals.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Substance Effect on HCl secretion
Histamine (H₂ receptor) ↑↑ HCl
Gastrin ↑ HCl
Acetylcholine ↑ HCl
Secretin ↓ HCl
GIP ↓ HCl

Exam pearl:
Histamine → H₂ receptor → parietal cell activation → gastric HCl secretion.

Physiology-03.question: ৪৪) Source of Pepsinogen
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Chief cell. Chief cells of the gastric glands secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of pepsin.

Mechanism:

  • Chief cells → Secrete pepsinogen

  • Parietal cells → Secrete HCl and intrinsic factor

  • HCl converts pepsinogen → pepsin

  • Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Parietal cell ✗ → Produces HCl and intrinsic factor, not pepsinogen.

  • G cell ✗ → Produces gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion.

  • EC cell (enterochromaffin cell) ✗ → Produces serotonin and other regulatory mediators.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Gastric cell Secretion
Chief cell Pepsinogen
Parietal cell HCl + Intrinsic factor
G cell Gastrin
ECL cell Histamine

Exam pearl:
Chief cells make pepsinogen; parietal cells make HCl.

Physiology-03.question: ৪৫) Which one is gold standard for measurement of GFR?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Inulin clearance. Inulin clearance is the gold standard method for measuring GFR because inulin is freely filtered by the glomerulus and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by renal tubules.

Ideal marker for GFR measurement:

  • Freely filtered

  • Not reabsorbed

  • Not secreted

  • Not metabolized by kidney

Inulin fulfills all these criteria.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Sodium clearance ✗ → Sodium is extensively reabsorbed, so it does not accurately reflect GFR.

  • Creatinine clearance ✗ → Commonly used clinically to estimate GFR, but slightly overestimates GFR due to tubular secretion.

  • Urea clearance ✗ → Urea is partially reabsorbed, so it underestimates GFR.

High-yield Renal recall:

Marker Use
Inulin clearance Gold standard for GFR
Creatinine clearance Clinical estimate of GFR
PAH clearance Renal plasma flow

Exam pearl:
Inulin = ideal filtration marker → gold standard measurement of GFR.

Physiology-03.question: ৪৬) Urea is the metabolic waste product of
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Protein. Urea is the major nitrogenous waste product formed from protein metabolism in the liver.

Mechanism:

  • Dietary proteins → amino acids

  • Amino acid breakdown → ammonia (NH₃)

  • Liver converts ammonia into urea through the urea cycle

  • Urea is excreted by the kidneys in urine

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Nucleic acid ✗ → Metabolized mainly to uric acid.

  • Creatine ✗ → Breakdown produces creatinine.

  • Haemoglobin ✗ → Breakdown produces bilirubin (from haem portion) and iron recycling.

High-yield Metabolism recall:

Substance Waste product
Protein Urea
Nucleic acid Uric acid
Creatine Creatinine
Haemoglobin Bilirubin

Exam pearl:
Protein metabolism → ammonia → urea (liver) → urine (kidney).

Physiology-03.question: ৪৭) Specific gravity of urine is low in
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is DI (Diabetes insipidus). Specific gravity of urine is low in DI because deficiency of ADH or renal resistance to ADH causes failure of water reabsorption, producing large amounts of dilute urine.

Key points:

  • Normal urine specific gravity: ~1.003–1.030

  • DI → ↓ ADH action → ↓ water reabsorption → dilute urine → low specific gravity

The other options are incorrect because:

  • DM ✗ → Usually increases urine specific gravity due to glucose in urine (glycosuria).

  • CRF ✗ → May cause impaired concentrating ability, but classic low specific gravity is seen in advanced renal failure with isosthenuria.

  • AKI ✗ → Specific gravity varies depending on the type and stage of injury.

High-yield Renal recall:

Condition Urine specific gravity
Diabetes insipidus Low
Diabetes mellitus High
Dehydration High
Advanced renal failure Fixed/isosthenuria

Exam pearl:
DI = dilute urine + low specific gravity due to lack of ADH effect.

Physiology-03.question: ৪৮) Presence of which particle in urine indicates UTI?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Nitrite. Presence of nitrite in urine is a marker of urinary tract infection (UTI), especially due to nitrate-reducing bacteria such as Enterobacteriaceae (e.g., E. coli).

Mechanism:

  • Dietary nitrate → converted to nitrite by bacterial nitrate reductase enzyme

  • Positive urine nitrite test suggests bacteriuria

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Glucose ✗ → Suggests diabetes mellitus or renal tubular problems, not UTI.

  • Protein ✗ → May occur in UTI but is not a specific marker.

  • Bile salt ✗ → Related to hepatobiliary disease, not UTI.

High-yield Renal recall:

Urine finding Suggests
Nitrite positive UTI (nitrate-reducing bacteria)
Leukocyte esterase Pyuria/UTI
Glucose Diabetes mellitus
Protein Renal disease

Exam pearl:
Urine nitrite positivity strongly suggests bacterial UTI, commonly E. coli.

Physiology-03.question: ৪৯) Digestion of proteins does not occur in
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Mouth. Protein digestion does not occur in the mouth because saliva does not contain proteolytic enzymes.

Sites of protein digestion:

  • Stomach → Pepsin starts protein digestion in acidic pH.

  • Small intestine → Major site of protein digestion by pancreatic enzymes (trypsin, chymotrypsin, peptidases).

  • Large intestine → No significant protein digestion; bacterial breakdown of residual proteins may occur.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Stomach ✗ → Protein digestion begins here by pepsin.

  • Small intestine ✗ → Main site of protein digestion and amino acid absorption.

  • Large intestine ✗ → Although not a major site, bacterial proteolysis can occur.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Site Protein digestion
Mouth Absent
Stomach Pepsin
Small intestine Trypsin, chymotrypsin, peptidases
Large intestine Minimal bacterial breakdown

Exam pearl:
Protein digestion starts in the stomach, not in the mouth.

Physiology-03.question: ৫০) Absorption of amino acid is slower in
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Ileum. Amino acid absorption is slower in the ileum compared with the jejunum, where most amino acid absorption occurs.

Key points:

  • Jejunum → Main site of amino acid absorption (rapid absorption)

  • Ileum → Absorption continues but at a slower rate

  • Stomach → Minimal amino acid absorption

  • Duodenum → Mainly receives pancreatic enzymes and begins digestion

The other options are less appropriate because:

  • Stomach ✗ → Very little amino acid absorption occurs, but the question usually refers to intestinal absorption rate.

  • Duodenum ✗ → Absorption occurs but is not the major site.

  • Jejunum ✗ → Site of rapid and major amino acid absorption.

High-yield GI physiology recall:

Site Amino acid absorption
Duodenum Begins
Jejunum Maximum & rapid
Ileum Slower
Large intestine Minimal

Exam pearl:
Jejunum = major site of amino acid absorption; ileum = slower absorption.
